{"decision":"RECORDED AS BRAINSTORMING, NOT AS A PROPOSAL. Anthony, 2026-08-24: *"what else is out there besides rocksdb that perfectly meets what reflow2 needs, but is much faster to compile than rocksdb?"*

═══════════════════════════════════════════════
📐 WHAT A REPLACEMENT ACTUALLY HAS TO DO — read from the code, not assumed

The seam is far narrower than "replace RocksDB" sounds. `KvBackend` (dynograph-storage/src/backend.rs) is **six byte-level primitives** over six named column families:

    get(cf, key) -> Option<Arc<[u8]>>      put(cf, key, value)
    delete(cf, key)                        prefix_scan(cf, prefix) -> Vec<(k,v)>
    prefix_delete(cf, prefix)              commit_batch(ops)

`ifc:kv-backend`'s own spec says everything schema-aware — validation, the reverse index, the read cache, the write-buffer overlay, the full-text sidecar — sits ABOVE this trait, and that **ordered prefix iteration is the one structural assumption**.

⭐⭐ AND IT ALREADY HAS TWO IMPLEMENTATIONS. Besides RocksDB there is an in-memory HashMap backend in the same file. **The swap this question asks about is already demonstrated once**, which makes this an unusually cheap thing to try — and is the sharpest difference from `dec:idea-swap-dynograph-foundation-as-the-substitutability-demo`, which was REJECTED for costing as much as the real thing. That node measured 48 files importing `dynograph_core`; this touches ONE file behind a six-function trait. **Its cost argument does not reach this question.**

⭐ THE FIT NOBODY HAS EXPLOITED: reflow2 is SINGLE-WRITER by design — the whole graph is held under a single-writer lock. RocksDB is a concurrent LSM built for many writers. An engine whose model IS single-writer/multi-reader is not a compromise here; it is a closer match than what is there.

═══════════════════════════════════════════════
🛑 THE PREMISE, MEASURED BEFORE ANSWERING — and it is only half true

Recorded because the question names compile time as the reason, and the reason is worth checking:

    release build of reflow2-mcp (~19 min)  — recompiled RocksDB: 0 times
    workspace test run #1 (~10 min)         — recompiled RocksDB: 0 times
    workspace test run #2 (~10 min)         — recompiled RocksDB: 0 times

Every long wait on 2026-08-24 was recompiling **reflow2-core and reflow2-mcp**, because they were being edited. RocksDB was cached throughout — reflow2's own Cargo.toml already calls it "a one-time, cached cost", and that holds.

⇒ **THE ANSWER MUST NAME WHICH COMPILE IT SPEEDS UP.** A cold first build, a CI cache miss, a new contributor's first `cargo build`, and a profile switch each pay the RocksDB cost in full — those are real and recurring. Day-to-day iteration does not, and a swap justified on day-to-day iteration would be justified on a cost that is not being paid.

⚠️ THE DISK COST IS UNCONTESTED THOUGH, and is a separate argument: one cached `librocksdb-sys` build directory measures **1.7 GB**. That compounds `[profile.dev]`'s own note about cargo having no GC.

═══════════════════════════════════════════════
IDEAS, UNRANKED, each with what it costs

**A. redb — pure Rust, ACID, ordered B-tree, single-writer/multi-reader.**
   ⭐ Named tables map to column families; ordered iteration is native; zero C or C++, so it compiles in seconds. Its concurrency model is EXACTLY reflow2's.
   ⚠️ Younger and less battle-tested than RocksDB; single file rather than a directory of SSTs, which changes what backup and the `.reflow2/graph` layout mean.

**B. fjall — pure Rust LSM, partitions ≈ column families.**
   ⭐ The closest SEMANTIC match: same shape as what is there, so the port is the most mechanical of the options.
   ⚠️ Also young — and being an LSM it inherits the compaction question that surfaced the same day (a live store at 7.4× the bytes of its content). Choosing it keeps that problem rather than dissolving it.

**C. LMDB via `heed` — small C, memory-mapped, single-writer/multi-reader.**
   ⭐ Decades of production use, named databases ≈ column families, ordered cursors, and it is SMALL — it compiles in seconds despite being C, so "it is C" and "it is slow to build" are not the same objection.
   ⚠️ The map size must be declared up front and grown deliberately; a write that outgrows it fails rather than expanding. Still a C dependency, which the pure-Rust options remove outright.

**D. libmdbx via `mdbx-rs` — LMDB's successor.**
   ⭐ Keeps C's virtues and fixes the map-size ergonomics that are LMDB's sharpest edge.
   ⚠️ A smaller community than any of the above; the bus factor is a real consideration for a store that holds the only copy of a design.

**E. sled — pure Rust, ordered, embedded.**
   ⚠️ Named for completeness rather than as a candidate: it has been pre-1.0 for years with a rewrite signalled. A design store is the wrong place to take that bet.

**F. SQLite via `rusqlite` (bundled) — and it could collapse TWO dependencies.**
   ⭐⭐ The interesting one, because SQLite's FTS5 could replace **tantivy** as well — the 847-line `dynograph-text` crate that increment 5 of the absorption would otherwise bring in. One dependency instead of two, and the most battle-tested storage engine in existence.
   ⚠️ A relational engine wearing a KV trait is a mismatch in spirit, and prefix scans become index scans; performance would have to be measured rather than assumed. Bundled SQLite is still a C compile, though a far smaller one.

**G. KEEP RocksDB AND ATTACK THE COST THAT IS ACTUALLY PAID.** sccache or a prebuilt artifact for cold/CI builds; or feature-gate it out of the builds that do not need it (`--no-default-features` already runs the core suite without it).
   ⭐ The honest status quo, and the only option that needs no port. It is also what the measurement above argues for if the pain is day-to-day iteration rather than cold builds.
   ⚠️ It does nothing for the disk cost, nothing for the C++ toolchain requirement, and nothing for a contributor's first build.

═══════════════════════════════════════════════
📌 WHAT NOBODY HAS COSTED, so the list is not read as an estimate

No measurement exists of a COLD build's RocksDB share (the number that would justify A-F), of any candidate's compile time in this tree, or of any candidate's read latency on a 3,100-node design. The seam's narrowness makes a spike genuinely cheap — one file, six functions, and an existing in-memory implementation to copy the shape from — so **the honest next step is to build one behind the trait and measure, rather than to choose from this list on paper.**

⚠️ AND A BOUND ON THE WHOLE QUESTION: `KvBackend` lives in dynograph-foundation, not reflow2. Until the absorption's increment 5 lands, changing it means changing somebody else's repository — which `dec:idea-dynograph-crates-independent-in-code-coupled-in-release` says reflow2's design has no standing to decide. **Absorb first, then swap** is the ordering that keeps this inside reflow2's own walls.","name":"OPEN — is there a byte store that meets the six-function KvBackend seam as well as RocksDB does, and compiles in seconds rather than minutes?","rationale":"Recorded via the brainstorm skill at `proposed`. Anthony thinking out loud, 2026-08-24, immediately after the RocksDB DEBUG_LEVEL exchange. Nothing here is intent and nothing is planned.

The premise was measured before the options were listed — not to argue the question down, but because it changes what a good answer has to be. "Faster to compile" is true of every option here for a COLD build and true of none of them for the iteration loop that was actually slow today.

DEDUP: read three near-matches in full. `dec:idea-swap-dynograph-foundation-as-the-substitutability-demo` is REJECTED and asks about reimplementing the whole foundation — its cost argument (48 files import dynograph_core) does not reach a six-function trait with an existing second implementation. `dec:absorb-the-foundation-subset-and-end-the-dependency` decides WHAT to absorb, not what the bytes land on. `dec:idea-where-does-the-10k-work-actually-land` already records that "the byte store is already swappable" and asks a scaling question instead.","status":"proposed"}
